slides.title: One summary button, three promises
keyPoints: Accept complete integer tokens only
Accept 1–1000 readings, each −100 through 100
Return a count and total only after all checks
slides.narration: Imagine three screens that all show a summary of inspection readings. Each screen has one button, but behind that button the program must read words, check their meaning, and add numbers. Our first job is to name what success promises. The text must contain whole integer tokens. The number of readings and each reading must fit the stated limits. Only then may we return a summary. This is a question about a trustworthy entrance to work, not about how many classes we can create. A user who supplies 4x should get rejection, not a cheerful total of four. We will locate exactly where each promise becomes true.
actions: Ask for one accepted input, one syntax error, and one domain error.

question.prompt: Why are 4x and 101 rejected for different reasons?
question.answer: 4x is not a complete integer token; 101 is an integer but exceeds the accepted domain.

slides.title: Start with one direct workflow
keyPoints: A fixed valid input needs no object hierarchy
Read, check, then calculate
This baseline does not prove complete-token parsing
slides.narration: This complete baseline uses a fixed input so we can see the order without a large interface. The stream reads integers into a vector, a growable sequence of values. We then reject a bad count, reject values outside the range, and finally calculate the total. The colon in the final loop means take each value from the vector in order. The program has no shared state and returns no reference into temporary storage. For the known input it works. Its input loop is not yet a sufficient parser for arbitrary user text: stream extraction can stop after reading a numeric prefix. Keep that limitation in mind before copying this code into several screens.
actions: Run the program, then predict whether replacing 6 4 with 6x would necessarily trigger rejection.
slides.sourceRef: Lecture demonstration for manuscript/ch10.json → A small request with several hidden steps

question.prompt: Why is this baseline unsuitable as a complete user-input contract?
question.answer: Its stream loop can accept a numeric prefix and stop. It does not establish that every token was consumed as a complete integer.

slides.title: Successful conversion can still reject the token
keyPoints: from_chars reports both status and stopping position
A numeric prefix is not a complete token
Check both conditions before storing the number
slides.narration: Here is a small, safe reproduction of the parsing trap. The text is 6x. The conversion function can read the six, so its error code reports success. It stops before the x. We print both facts separately rather than pretending that successful conversion means valid input. A pointer is a value that identifies a position in storage. The end pointer identifies the position after the final character; we compare with it but do not read a character there. The repaired decision requires no conversion error and a stopping pointer equal to the end. The main chapter parser uses that same two-part rule before it adds an integer to its vector.
actions: Pause before running and ask learners to predict all three lines.
slides.sourceRef: Lecture demonstration for manuscript/ch10.json → Parsing must consume the whole token

question.prompt: Which extra condition rejects 6x even when ec reports success?
question.answer: The stopping pointer must equal the end pointer. For 6x, it points at x instead.

slides.title: Repeated call order is the pressure for a facade
keyPoints: Clients request a checked summary
Importer owns the sequence
Subsystem operations remain focused
slides.narration: Suppose a second screen copies our direct workflow but forgets validation. A third screen validates only after adding the numbers. Every screen now carries a slightly different version of the same promise. A facade is a simpler public entrance to a related group of operations. Importer::run becomes that entrance: clients ask for a checked summary and the method controls the sequence. The double colon names a member within its class. This design does not need inheritance or a virtual method. The parser, validator, and summarizer remain concrete tools. A free function could provide the same facade when no stored state or configuration is needed.
actions: Have learners name the workflow in one sentence without listing internal method names.
slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch10.json → A small doorway rather than a new object hierarchy

question.prompt: Why would forwarding every subsystem method leave the original problem unsolved?
question.answer: Callers would still need to know the correct sequence and establish every precondition themselves.

slides.title: The contract we must preserve
keyPoints: Parse complete whitespace-separated integer tokens.
Accept 1–1000 values, each from -100 through 100.
Return count and total only after validation.
slides.narration:
A checked reading summary. One facade method fixes the call order while member objects retain separate parsing, validation, and calculation responsibilities. No polymorphism is needed.

Parse complete whitespace-separated integer tokens. Accept 1–1000 values, each from -100 through 100. Return count and total only after validation.

Malformed tokens never become accepted partial integers. Summarizer is reached only after Validator accepts the vector. Returned Stats owns values and does not refer to local storage. These are the rules that define a correct extension, even if it has the right C++ types. A free function performing the same sequence is an equally valid facade for a stateless subsystem. Letting every screen call the services directly is reasonable only when callers genuinely need different workflows and can enforce their preconditions.

question.prompt: Which promise would a new Facade implementation be allowed to break?
question.answer: None of the stated requirements. The implementation may change, but these rules remain: Malformed tokens never become accepted partial integers. Summarizer is reached only after Validator accepts the vector. Returned Stats owns values and does not refer to local storage.

slides.title: A small request with several hidden steps
keyPoints: An inspection screen accepts whitespace-separated integer readings and displays their count and total.
The simplest implementation for one screen is a direct sequence: parse text, validate the vector, then summarize it.
slides.narration:
An inspection screen accepts whitespace-separated integer readings and displays their count and total. Each reading must be between -100 and 100. There must be at least one reading and at most one thousand. Tokens such as 4x and 1.5 are invalid. The screen should ask for a summary, not repeat parsing rules and subsystem call order in every event handler.

The simplest implementation for one screen is a direct sequence: parse text, validate the vector, then summarize it. That is a reasonable function, and the pattern does not require making it a class. Trouble begins when several screens repeat the sequence. One may forget validation. Another may summarize first, so invalid data reaches arithmetic. A third may accept a valid prefix of a malformed token. The application's simple request has become tied to the details of three services.

question.prompt: Why should a caller not have to remember parsing, validation and summary order for every import?
question.answer: A caller may forget a gate or summarize invalid input. One checked entry point can keep that required order consistent while returning the result the caller actually needs.

slides.title: A small doorway rather than a new object hierarchy
keyPoints: A facade is a simpler public entrance to a set of related operations.
The facade gives a name to a useful application operation: import readings and produce a valid summary.
The component classes here make the boundary visible in a complete small program.
slides.narration:
A facade is a simpler public entrance to a set of related operations. Importer::run accepts text and returns Stats. Internally it performs the required steps in the required order. It does not introduce inheritance because no interchangeable family of importers is needed. Parser, Validator, and Summarizer are ordinary member objects. Their lifetimes are part of Importer itself.

The facade gives a name to a useful application operation: import readings and produce a valid summary. It does not merely rename every subsystem method. A facade with parse, validate, summarize, configure_parser, configure_validator, and many other forwarded operations would force everyday callers to understand the old sequencing problem again. Advanced callers can still use the smaller subsystem types directly when they accept those responsibilities.

The component classes here make the boundary visible in a complete small program. In a tiny project, these could be free functions and run could be the facade function. The reason to keep the boundary is consistency of use; the decision to store member objects is separate. A larger subsystem might keep parser options or other state in these members, but this example does not invent state just to justify classes.

slides.title: Parsing must consume the whole token
keyPoints: Parser first uses istringstream to split on whitespace.
For each token, std::from_chars tries to read a base-ten integer into n.
The end pointer is token.data() plus token.size(): the position just after the final character.
This narrow grammar accepts a leading minus sign and ordinary decimal digits.
slides.narration:
Parser first uses istringstream to split on whitespace. The extraction expression input >> token succeeds when it obtains another string token. The while loop continues only on success. An empty or whitespace-only input therefore returns an empty vector; deciding whether that count is acceptable belongs to Validator.

For each token, std::from_chars tries to read a base-ten integer into n. Its result contains an error code, ec, and a pointer, ptr, marking where parsing stopped. Success requires both no error and ptr equal to the token's end. Parsing 4x can read the integer 4 successfully but stops at x, so the second condition rejects it. Parsing an integer outside the representable int range sets an error. The code never uses n unless both checks pass.

The end pointer is token.data() plus token.size(): the position just after the final character. That position is valid for comparison and as an end marker, but it is not a character the parser should dereference. data supplies contiguous character storage, and from_chars borrows it only during the call. Parser stores the integer value in its vector, not a pointer into token. Reusing token on the next loop iteration is therefore safe.

This narrow grammar accepts a leading minus sign and ordinary decimal digits. Integer from_chars does not accept a leading plus sign. Whitespace is handled outside it by the stream. The contract intentionally does not accept decimal fractions, thousands separators, or locale-specific numbers. If those become requirements, update the grammar and tests explicitly instead of hoping a different conversion function happens to accept them.

slides.title: Validation establishes arithmetic assumptions
keyPoints: Validator checks count before checking each value.
Summarizer relies on that validated-input precondition.
Importer enforces the precondition by calling validate before summarize.
This is not an automatic transaction mechanism.
slides.narration:
Validator checks count before checking each value. The count must be in the closed range one through one thousand, and each value must be in the closed range -100 through 100. Closed means both endpoints are allowed. With those limits, a total lies between -100000 and 100000. That is well within int on the supported compiler environment, which uses at least 32-bit int for these examples.

Summarizer relies on that validated-input precondition. A precondition is a rule the caller must make true before calling an operation. Its local total begins at zero and adds each value exactly once. Stats stores the number of values as std::size_t and the total as int. The brace return {v.size(), total} initializes these members in their declared order. It does not attach references to the input vector.

Importer enforces the precondition by calling validate before summarize. If parsing or validation throws, control leaves run immediately; calculation is skipped and no Stats value is returned. The input string remains unchanged. The local vector is destroyed when the function exits normally or because of an exception. Because this example has no external writes, failure cannot leave a half-written file or partially updated database.

This is not an automatic transaction mechanism. A facade that writes to two files can still fail after writing the first. Such a workflow needs a separate recovery or commit design. A simple public method reduces caller complexity; it does not erase the failure modes of the operations it coordinates.

slides.title: Compilation, performance, and a maintainable boundary
keyPoints: All calls in this example are direct calls to concrete types.
The one-thousand count check protects the calculation, but parsing still builds the vector before validation.
When replacing a parser, keep the facade's accepted grammar and rejected cases stable unless a requirement changes.
The key debugging question is where a guarantee is established.
slides.narration:
All calls in this example are direct calls to concrete types. The compiler checks signatures and may inline small methods. No virtual dispatch or heap-based object hierarchy is needed. The vector may allocate while collecting input, and strings and streams manage their own storage. At execution, values move from text tokens to integers to a checked summary. Control follows the three-stage sequence shown in the diagram.

The one-thousand count check protects the calculation, but parsing still builds the vector before validation. This is acceptable for the bounded local example and is not a denial-of-service defense for unlimited network input. A production ingestion service should stop reading after its token or byte limit, before allocating for the entire request. That change belongs at the input boundary and needs tests of the chosen maximum.

When replacing a parser, keep the facade's accepted grammar and rejected cases stable unless a requirement changes. When adding a new summary, decide whether it belongs in Stats or deserves another operation. Avoid turning Importer into a giant class that manages screens, persistence, authentication, and printing. A useful facade has one coherent purpose. Separate facades can expose other workflows over the same subsystem without making every client know every service.

The key debugging question is where a guarantee is established. Parser establishes valid integer syntax. Validator establishes domain and count bounds. Summarizer assumes those bounds. Importer connects them. If an invalid value reaches arithmetic, inspect the call order and the bypass paths rather than adding random checks to the output screen.

question.prompt: Why can a successful mean test miss malformed-token bugs?
question.answer: An ordinary numeric string never exercises the parser's end pointer. Test junk suffixes and fractional tokens separately from arithmetic results.

slides.title: Each stage establishes the next stage’s permission
keyPoints: Parser establishes integer syntax
Validator establishes count and value bounds
Summarizer relies on both established facts
slides.narration: A precondition is a rule that must already be true before an operation begins. The summarizer has one: this vector has passed validation. It does not independently rediscover that fact. The facade supplies the missing proof by calling the validator first. This matters for arithmetic, not just friendly error messages. At most one thousand numbers, each between negative one hundred and positive one hundred, place the total between negative one hundred thousand and positive one hundred thousand. That fits the supported environment's integer type. If someone calls Summarizer directly with unchecked data, the class name does not protect them. Debugging starts by finding the path that bypassed the promise.
actions: Ask learners to derive both total bounds aloud before showing the answer.

question.prompt: Does moving validation after summarize preserve safety if an error is eventually thrown?
question.answer: No. The arithmetic has already run without its precondition; a later exception cannot undo undefined signed overflow.

slides.title: Borrow input; own the result
keyPoints: const reference reads the caller’s string
run owns its local vector
Stats contains independent count and total values
slides.narration: Follow storage as well as control. The const reference parameter lets run read the caller's string without copying it and without changing it through this parameter. The parser returns a vector of integer values. Run keeps that vector as a local object, and the validator and summarizer borrow it while they execute. Stats then copies out a count and a total; it does not point into the vector. When run finishes, the local vector can be destroyed without harming the returned summary. The Importer member objects also live with Importer. There is no reason to introduce manual allocation merely to connect three ordinary operations.
actions: Draw separate labels for borrowed text, owned local vector, and returned value.
slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch10.json → A small doorway rather than a new object hierarchy

question.prompt: Would returning a reference to the local vector be safe after run returns?
question.answer: No. The vector is destroyed at function exit; a reference to it would outlive the object it names.

slides.title: Exceptions skip later stages, not earlier side effects
keyPoints: Failure prevents a Stats result
Local owned storage is cleaned up
A facade is not automatically a transaction
slides.narration: If parsing throws an exception, ordinary execution leaves run at that point. Validation and summarizing do not happen. If validation throws, summarizing is skipped. C++ destroys the local objects whose lifetimes end during this exit, so the vector does not need a manual cleanup branch. That is a useful failure guarantee, but be precise about its scope. This example has no writes to a file or database. If a future facade first writes one file and then fails while writing another, an exception will not restore the first file. All-or-nothing external work requires a separate commit or recovery design. A short interface does not erase side effects.
actions: Propose a write-first workflow and ask which effects an exception can undo automatically.

question.prompt: What observable result does run return for whitespace-only input?
question.answer: It returns no Stats value; parsing yields an empty vector and validation throws.

slides.title: Compile-time checking cannot prove the workflow contract
keyPoints: The compiler checks available functions and types
Execution checks actual tokens and bounds
Resource limits must be enforced early enough
slides.narration: The compiler can reject a call with the wrong type or a method name that does not exist. It does not prove that calling summarize before validate respects this program's intended policy. Both calls can be well-typed in the wrong order. Tests therefore need to exercise actual malformed text, edge values, empty input, and count limits. There is another boundary worth finding: parsing builds the entire vector before the validator checks the one-thousand limit. That limits accepted calculations but does not limit work spent reading a huge input. A network-facing service should enforce byte or token limits while reading. The current bounded teaching example makes no stronger resource guarantee.
actions: Ask which check rejects 1001 tokens and whether that check prevented their allocation.
slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch10.json → Compilation, performance, and a maintainable boundary

question.prompt: Why is a post-parse count check insufficient to bound memory used by arbitrary incoming text?
question.answer: The vector and tokens may already have been allocated before the validator sees their count.

slides.title: A mean should reuse the established contract
keyPoints: Call run to retain one acceptance rule
Convert before division
A valid count is already nonzero
slides.narration: The lab adds a mean, which is the total divided by the number of readings. This is a good extension because it asks whether we trust our existing entrance enough to reuse it. Mean calls run and receives Stats only after all old checks succeed. It then converts the total to double before division. Double stores a floating-point approximation and can represent halves in this example. Dividing integer nine by integer two first would produce integer four; converting that four later cannot recover the lost half. Empty input still throws because run rejects it. A separate parsing path for mean would create a second contract to keep synchronized.
actions: Compare converting before division with converting the finished integer quotient.

question.prompt: Why does mean not need its own special empty-vector branch?
question.answer: run rejects empty input before returning Stats, so every successful result has a count of at least one.

slides.narration:
A facade offers one useful entrance to a subsystem. A simple entrance does not require inheritance. Validate complete tokens rather than accepting numeric prefixes. Call order can establish the preconditions of later stages. A facade does not automatically make external side effects atomic.

Expose one coherent workflow while keeping subsystem preconditions documented. A small facade gives callers a stable place to depend on during library changes.

question.prompt: Explain Facade without reciting its class names.
question.answer: One facade method fixes the call order while member objects retain separate parsing, validation, and calculation responsibilities. No polymorphism is needed. A free function performing the same sequence is an equally valid facade for a stateless subsystem. Letting every screen call the services directly is reasonable only when callers genuinely need different workflows and can enforce their preconditions.

slides.title: Choose the boundary size, not the class count
keyPoints: One facade should name one coherent task
Direct subsystem access can remain available
A free function can be enough
slides.narration: A good facade is small in what callers must understand, not necessarily small in how much useful work it performs. Import readings is a coherent task. Import readings, manage users, render screens, send mail, and repair the database would be unrelated work gathered under one name. When requirements expand, ask which callers need which promise. A troubleshooting screen may reasonably use Parser alone to inspect raw tokens, as long as it understands that domain validation has not happened. That does not require weakening run for every other screen. Choose a separate, honestly named operation. For a stateless three-function subsystem, keep the free-function option on the table.
actions: Have pairs propose one feature that belongs in Importer and one that deserves another boundary.

question.prompt: Should a parse-only screen force run to accept out-of-range values?
question.answer: No. Keep run as a checked-summary operation and expose a distinct parse-only operation with a weaker documented promise.

slides.title: Debug the earliest broken promise
keyPoints: 4x accepted: inspect token consumption
Empty input totals zero: inspect count validation
Wrong mean: inspect arithmetic conversion order
slides.narration: Use the symptom to identify the earliest missing promise. If 4x becomes four, inspect the parser's end-position check. If no readings become count zero and total zero, inspect validation or a route that bypassed it. If a mean of four and five becomes four, inspect the division types. Adding an output-screen patch for each symptom hides the contract break and duplicates policy. The strongest regression tests describe both successful boundaries and specific rejection behavior. Include a single zero reading so nobody confuses a legitimate total of zero with absence of readings. Tests should explain the difference, not merely print a green status.
actions: Present the three symptoms one at a time and ask for the first source location to inspect.
slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch10.json → Parsing must consume the whole token

question.prompt: Why test both run("0") and run("")?
question.answer: The first is one valid reading with total zero; the second has no readings and must be rejected.

slides.title: Recall the entrance and its limits
keyPoints: Intent: simplify a useful subsystem workflow
Mechanism: ordered delegation
Guarantee: a successful result satisfies the declared contract
slides.narration: Explain Facade to a teammate without drawing a box first. We had several operations whose order mattered, and repeated clients were getting the order wrong. We introduced one useful entrance that applies the order once. The parser owns syntax, the validator owns accepted bounds, and the summarizer owns calculation under those bounds. The facade joins those responsibilities without pretending they are the same responsibility. It does not require a hierarchy, does not make every lower-level operation safe to call blindly, and does not make external writes atomic. In a code review, point to the invariant and the line where it is established. That explanation is more useful than merely naming the pattern.
actions: Ask for a thirty-second explanation using the words promise, order, and result.
